findings.claim: Chewy mound of shredded coconut, often dipped in chocolate
findings.because: This trap is a true description of another card on the roster, fd_0239 (the coconut macaroon). That confusion is already carried by confusedWithTerms, so it cannot also be a trap.
findings.fix: says: "Crisp rolled wafer of almond and butter, curled while still warm"; why: "It is a pair of smooth, domed almond shells joined by a filling."

findings.claim: Sweet custard of egg yolks and cream, baked until set and firm
findings.because: This is a true description of roster cards Pot de Crème (fd_0263) and Custard (fd_0250). A trap may not describe another card truly.
findings.fix: says: "Whole eggs and flour whipped into a light sponge, baked in a tall pan"; why: "It is whipped whites and sugar only, with no yolk or flour."

findings.claim: Baked, it goes crisp and melts away; toasted on a pie, it stays soft like marshmallow.
findings.because: The guest line may not use semicolons. Hard rule.
findings.fix: Baked, it goes crisp and melts away. Toasted on a pie, it stays soft like marshmallow.

findings.claim: Liguria, Italy. From the Latin for hearth
findings.because: Focaccia is baked all over Italy, and its roots go back to Roman panis focacius. Liguria (Genoa) is the most famous style, not the origin of focaccia as a whole. The hearth etymology (Latin focus) is correct.
findings.fix: Italy, famed in Liguria. Latin for hearth

findings.claim: usually baked empty first so it stays crisp, then filled
findings.because: Only tarts with wet or unbaked fillings (curd, cream, fresh fruit) are blind baked. Many classic tarts, such as frangipane, custard-fruit and apple tarts, bake with the filling already in. "Usually" overstates it.
findings.fix: often baked empty first so it stays crisp, then filled

findings.claim: blind-baking-and-pie-doctrine
findings.because: That entry is a technique essay about baking crusts empty and about pie doctrine. It is not the long-form entry on tarts as a dish, and the slug is meant only when the essay covers this same subject.
findings.fix: omit lexiconSlug

findings.claim: Baked, it goes crisp and melts away; toasted on a pie, it stays soft like marshmallow.
findings.because: The guest line may not hold a semicolon. A new hire reading it aloud also runs out of breath before the second half.
findings.fix: Baked, it turns crisp and melts away. Toasted on a pie, it stays soft like marshmallow.

findings.claim: It's an Italian flatbread baked in a pan with lots of olive oil, so the bottom fries crisp and the inside stays soft, usually with salt and rosemary on top.
findings.because: It is one 155-character sentence held together by 'so', 'and' and 'usually'. A nervous server loses the thread partway through, and it sounds like it is being read off a card.
findings.fix: It's an Italian flatbread baked in lots of olive oil, crisp on the bottom and soft inside, usually topped with salt and rosemary.

findings.claim: made with almond and filled with ganache, buttercream or jam
findings.because: 'Made with almond' is awkward to say aloud and does not tell the guest what the shell is. The shell is almond meringue, and naming it is what separates this from the coconut macaroon a guest may be expecting.
findings.fix: It's a little French sandwich cookie of almond meringue, crisp outside and chewy inside, filled with ganache, buttercream or jam.

findings.claim: Pistachio and raspberry macarons, three for the table
findings.because: 'Three for the table' is how a server talks, not how a menu is written. Real menus list the flavors, or a count and a price.
findings.fix: Pistachio and raspberry macarons

findings.claim: With no butter and little or no flour, it eats dense, moist and chewy
findings.because: States an absence of butter and flour that a server will repeat as a no-dairy or no-wheat assurance. Many recipes hold condensed milk, some add a spoon of flour, and some are butter-brushed or chocolate-dipped. Name the binder instead.
findings.fix: Bound by egg white and sugar, it eats dense, moist and chewy

findings.claim: "coconut", "egg white", "sugar", "often condensed milk", "sometimes chocolate"
findings.because: Many American coconut macaroon recipes add a little wheat flour to bind them, and a guest avoiding wheat needs that flagged, especially once the why no longer says there is little or none.
findings.fix: coconut, egg white, sugar, often condensed milk, sometimes wheat flour, sometimes chocolate

findings.claim: with no yolk or cream
findings.because: A trap's why may not state an absence. Some meringue desserts are finished with cream or folded into yolk mixtures, so 'no yolk or cream' reads as an assurance. Say what it is instead.
findings.fix: It is whites whipped with sugar into an airy foam, not a baked yolk custard.

findings.claim: "wheat flour", "butter", "sugar", "egg", "often cream"
findings.because: Classic tart shells (pâte sucrée) are often made with ground almond, and frangipane is a standard tart filling. A guest with a tree-nut allergy needs that flagged.
findings.fix: wheat flour, butter, sugar, egg, often cream, sometimes almond

findings.claim: German and Austrian, from the word for a round layered cake
findings.because: German Torte comes from Italian torta, from Late Latin torta, a round loaf of bread. The source word never meant a layered cake.
findings.fix: German and Austrian, via Italian torta, a round cake or loaf

findings.claim: A torte is cake all the way through.
findings.because: Linzer torte, a classic torte and one of this card's recipe candidates, is a nut-pastry shell with jam under a lattice. It is built like a tart, so the absolute rule is false for it.
findings.fix: Not a tart, which is a pastry shell holding a filling. Most tortes are layered cake throughout.

findings.claim: "sugar", "sometimes almond"
findings.because: Many classic Limousin and bistro clafoutis recipes add kirsch, which is alcohol and needs flagging for a guest. Sugar is not a flag item, so it can give up its slot. The list is already at the 7-item cap.
findings.fix: replace "sugar" with "often kirsch" (keep "sometimes almond")

findings.claim: baked with no pan so it browns crisp all round
findings.because: A free-form galette is baked on a flat baking sheet. It skips the tart pan, not every pan, so a new hire would repeat something false.
findings.fix: baked flat on a sheet, no tart ring, so it browns crisp all round

findings.claim: "often fruit"
findings.because: The galette des rois, a puff-pastry galette filled with almond frangipane, is the third common menu galette and is everywhere in January. The list has no almond to flag it for a guest with a nut allergy. Fruit is not a flag item.
findings.fix: replace "often fruit" with "sometimes almond"

findings.claim: A soufflé is baked and served hot.
findings.because: A frozen soufflé (soufflé glacé) is a common dessert-menu item. It is a mousse or parfait set cold in a collared dish and is never baked, so the absolute claim fails on menus that list one.
findings.fix: A hot soufflé is baked; a frozen one is really a mousse.

findings.claim: It's baked to order and comes out tall, golden and airy, with a soft, creamy middle. It's worth the wait, and it's best eaten the moment it lands.
findings.because: The line never answers "what is that?". It doesn't say it is an egg dish, or that it can be savory (cheese) or sweet (chocolate, vanilla), so the guest still doesn't know what they would be ordering.
findings.fix: It's a baked egg dish, cheese or chocolate, that rises tall and airy with a soft, creamy middle. It's made to order, so it's worth the wait.

findings.claim: ready to be filled with cream or cheese
findings.because: Savory choux puts the cheese in the dough (gougères). The puffs are not usually filled with cheese, so a guest who hears "filled with cheese" gets the wrong picture.
findings.fix: ready to be filled with cream or something savory

findings.claim: paht ah SHOO
findings.because: The respelling key wants hyphens between syllables and one capitalized stress per word. As written, "paht" and "ah" are separate words with no stress, and a dining room says the phrase as one run.
findings.fix: paht-ah-SHOO

findings.claim: you get in a mille-feuille or a beef Wellington
findings.because: A nervous new hire will stumble on "mille-feuille", and many American guests won't know it. The American menu name for the same pastry is napoleon.
findings.fix: you get in a napoleon or a beef Wellington

findings.claim: gah-LET
findings.because: An American dining room reduces the unstressed first syllable, so it is said guh-LET. The key has "uh" for exactly this.
findings.fix: guh-LET

findings.claim: "wheat flour", "butter", "water", "salt"
findings.because: Puff pastry is almost always brushed with beaten egg before baking for its gloss, so a guest avoiding egg is served egg even though the dough itself has none. The list reads as if egg is absent. The list has room for one more item.
findings.fix: "wheat flour", "butter", "water", "salt", "often egg wash"

findings.claim: "often fruit" ... "sometimes egg"
findings.because: The best-known French galette on a dessert menu is the galette des rois: puff pastry filled with almond frangipane. The list never flags nuts. Egg is also usual, both as the wash on the crust and cracked onto the Breton galette complète, so "sometimes" undersells it. The list is already at 7 items, so the fix swaps out fruit, which a guest can see on the plate.
findings.fix: replace "often fruit" with "sometimes almond", and "sometimes egg" with "often egg"

findings.claim: "often sugar"
findings.because: Sweet soufflés are classically flavored with liqueur (Grand Marnier, kirsch), and alcohol is something a guest needs flagged. Sugar is not an allergy concern, and the list is already at 7 items.
findings.fix: "sometimes liqueur"

findings.claim: "sometimes almond"
findings.because: Many clafoutis recipes add kirsch or another liqueur to the batter or the fruit, and a guest avoiding alcohol would need that flagged. The list has room for it.
findings.fix: add "sometimes kirsch"

findings.claim: Many swap some or all of the flour for ground nuts or crumbs
findings.because: "all of the flour" invites a server to tell a guest avoiding wheat that the torte has no flour. The crumbs in question are usually breadcrumbs, which are wheat, and most tortes keep some flour. What a torte holds is for the madeWith list and the kitchen to say, not the why.
findings.fix: Many replace part of the flour with ground nuts or crumbs

findings.claim: Torte overstates layering. The gist says 'layered cake' flat out, and notThis says 'Most tortes are layered cake throughout'. On American menus a torte is very often a single-layer cake: flourless chocolate torte, or a nut torte like the card's own line and recipe (oregon-hazelnut-torte). Linzer torte, one of the recipe candidates, is a lattice pastry and not a layer cake at all. A server who repeats 'layers' will describe a torte that does not match the plate. The gist is also 70 characters, the longest gist in the section and 5 over its only trap.

Pâté is on the roster (cured section), but Pâte à Choux has only Puff Pastry in confusedWithTerms, and its notThis does not warn against the mix-up.

Pâté is on the roster (cured section), but Pâte à Choux has only Puff Pastry in confusedWithTerms, and its notThis does not warn against the mix-up.

findings.claim: "It's egg whites whipped with sugar into a glossy foam. Baked, it turns crisp and melts away. Toasted on a pie, it stays soft like marshmallow."
findings.because: Three sentences; a guest line is two at most, and the contract refused it.
findings.fix: The last two sentences joined with and; no fact changed.

critic.notes:
Coverage check. All 15 roster rows have a card. The section mean is 650 chars per card, under the 720 ceiling, and the longest card is Soufflé at 741. I found no verdict words, banned substrings, dashes or temperatures. Each guest line answers 'what is that?'. The Macaroon knownPacketError is covered: its trap 'Two little sponge cakes sandwiched...' matches /sandwich/i and does not describe the Macaron card. Every confusion inside the section is linked both ways: Macaron/Macaroon, Tart/Torte, Tart/Galette, Choux/Puff. Soufflé/Mousse is linked across sections.

Length parity. On 9 of the 13 single-trap cards the gist is longer than the trap, by 2 to 5 chars. Examples: Beignets 65/60, Focaccia 69/64, Sourdough 65/62, Tart 66/62, Puff Pastry 66/62, Pavlova 68/62. Everything is within 10 chars, but with only one trap per card the gist is usually the longest option, so trimming 3 to 5 chars off those gists would remove the tell.

Optional polish:
(1) Galette: add 'Buckwheat' (starches) to seeAlsoTerms, since the Breton meaning is a buckwheat crepe.
(2) Macaron: 'mah-kah-ROHN' rhymes the last syllable with 'loan'. An American dining room more often says 'mah-kuh-RAHN', and that version also sets it further apart from 'mack-uh-ROON'.
(3) Two traps describe a sweet crepe: Beignets 'Thin French pancakes folded around sugar, fruit or chocolate' and Clafoutis 'Thin French pancake folded around fruit and cream'. They are close to each other and sit near Galette's buckwheat-crepe meaning. They do not strictly describe the Galette card, which is savory buckwheat, but rewording one would reduce the overlap.

findings.claim: baked low until dry
findings.because: That is how a plain meringue is baked (around 100 C for an hour or more). A dacquoise is baked hotter and shorter, typically 160 to 180 C (320 to 355 F) for 15 to 30 minutes, and is pulled while the inside is still soft; baking it dry would give exactly the brittle, hollow texture the notThis says it is not.
findings.fix: baked until just set

findings.claim: Light sponge cake soaked in syrup and layered with buttercream
findings.because: A syrup-soaked sponge layered with buttercream is a fair description of many tortes, and Torte (fd_0242) is on this roster (its packet line reads 'cake filled with whipped cream, buttercreams, jams'). A trap may not be a true description of another card; a génoise, which is not on the roster, keeps the same wrong idea without the collision.
findings.fix: Airy sponge of whole eggs, flour and melted butter, cut into layers

findings.claim: A thin batter of milk, egg yolks, flour
findings.because: The classic Bordeaux batter uses whole eggs plus extra yolks (the standard formulas run two whole eggs and two yolks to half a liter of milk), not yolks alone. 'eggs' is true of every version.
findings.fix: A thin batter of milk, eggs, flour

findings.claim: egg yolk
findings.because: Whole eggs and yolks both go into the classic batter, so the flag should be the whole egg, not the yolk; a white-only reaction is rare but real and 'egg' covers both.
findings.fix: egg

findings.claim: Thin Breton pancake folded around melted butter and sugar
findings.because: A Breton pancake folded around butter and sugar is the beurre-sucre crêpe or galette, and Galette (fd_0246) is on this roster with Buckwheat as its lexicon candidate, so a reader who has learned that card could take this trap as true of it. Gâteau Breton, not on the roster, keeps the 'Breton butter thing' confusion without the collision.
findings.fix: Dense Breton butter cake baked from a smooth creamed batter

findings.claim: made with salted butter
findings.because: Salted butter is the mark of the Breton version only. A plain sablé (pâte sablée, sablé normand, sablés de Caen) is made with unsalted butter and a pinch of salt, and the card's term is Sablé in general, with Breton as an alias. The why already draws the distinction; the guest line should not erase it.
findings.fix: often with salted butter

findings.claim: Cold butter is worked into flour and sugar with an egg yolk
findings.because: That is the sablage method and it does explain the name, but the Breton version the next sentence describes is made the other way, by creaming soft salted butter with sugar and yolks and adding flour last, usually with a little baking powder. As written the card implies one method for both.
findings.fix: Butter is rubbed or creamed into flour and sugar with an egg yolk

findings.claim: It's a Breton butter pastry,
findings.because: A guest, and most third-day servers, do not know that Breton means from Brittany; the guest line should open on a word anyone at the table understands, and origin already names Douarnenez and Brittany.
findings.fix: It's a French butter pastry,

findings.claim: Thin Breton pancake folded around melted butter and sugar
findings.because: That is a true description of the Breton crepe galette (butter and sugar is its classic sweet filling), and Galette (fd_0246) is on this section's roster with Buckwheat as its lexicon candidate, so the trap could be accepted for another card. A trap must be false of every card.
findings.fix: Dense butter cake from Brittany with a sugar glaze brushed on top

findings.claim: It's a French butter shortbread, crisp and crumbly, made with salted butter. Here it's the crunchy base under the fruit and cream.
findings.because: "Here it's the crunchy base under the fruit and cream" assumes one plating; the card must work when the sable is a cookie among the mignardises or under ice cream, and a server repeating it at the wrong table describes a dish that is not in front of the guest. "butter" is also said twice in one breath.
findings.fix: It's a French shortbread, crisp and crumbly, made with salted butter. It's often the crunchy base under fruit and cream.

findings.claim: Strawberries, Sablé breton, crème fraîche, basil
findings.because: The alias is written "Sablé Breton"; the line must carry the term or an alias as written, and a real menu prints it either all lowercase mid-line or fully capitalized, never "Sablé breton".
findings.fix: Strawberries, sablé breton, crème fraîche, basil

findings.claim: so little gluten forms and the baked cookie breaks into fine sandy crumbs
findings.because: True as baking science, but a new server will repeat "little gluten" to a guest asking about gluten, and it is made with wheat flour. The tenderness mechanism can be stated without naming gluten at all.
findings.fix: so it stays tender and the baked cookie breaks into fine sandy crumbs

findings.claim: There is no chocolate in it.
findings.because: A free-from assurance. Chocolate canelés are a real variation some kitchens make, so the flat claim is not even reliably true. State what it is, not what it lacks.
findings.fix: It is not chocolate cake.

findings.claim: and there is no caramel in it.
findings.because: A free-from assurance in the house-banned pattern, and caramel sablés exist. Refute the trap on form, not on absence of an ingredient.
findings.fix: and it is not a caramel wafer.

findings.claim: There is no flour sponge in it.
findings.because: "No flour" is the phrase a server carries away, while the card's own madeWith says sometimes wheat flour. Refute the sponge, not the flour.
findings.fix: It is not a sponge cake.
